title: After the Banner Band: Lafayette, writing and teaching
summary: Duhé broke up the Black Eagle to reinforce the Banner Band, then led a five-piece band in Lafayette, wrote three songs and taught local players.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: When was your last band about then? After the Banner band, did you give up playing dances

and just start teaching or writing? After the Banner, after the Banner we, at least, I was with the Black Eagle before I joined the band. That's the way it happened. We decided to break the Black Eagle up to reinforce the Banner band, which we did. And I took Ike Tomlin and went to New Iberic. And then the high stage they ever saw. And I came here and organized a little five-piece band right here. I had Frank Brown and Joe and Drum and Bo Frey and Clifton who was playing the banjo. He was in the French Quarter. I played plenty of banjo. Very good. I had Bill Newton on the bass. I had a pretty good five-reggie education right here. Good one. So you're writing songs now? I'm not, not no more. I wrote three. You have written songs. I wrote three and stopped, but I got two in the trunk. They're supposed to be some word added to it. I'm not ready for writing words now. I'm trying to see how those three are going to take out. Do you do any teaching now? I taught one to Professor Roger that, the Reed section right there at Professor Paul Grove School here, the Reed section. And I taught Gobert a couple of players around him, Abraham, the banjo.
Are there any good old style bands here around in this part of the country anymore? No. The trombonist Gus, I can't remember his last name. Point net.
I have his band. Oh yeah, the band. Still got the band of band here. I guess you call it something else but it. I heard them but... He still play, play the piano trombone.
Yes, he's very good. He's playing right now?
Yeah. Trombone, bartending the day for the piano.
